intro: Sintra doesn't grow old trees so much as collect them. Nineteenth century estate owners, chasing the Romantic idea of a mountain retreat, filled the town's palace gardens with specimens shipped in from every continent they could reach: a New Zealand pohutukawa, a Norfolk Island pine, a Pacific cedar that has spent a century and a half quietly walking across its own lawn. Beneath that imported spectacle, Sintra's own native cork oak, three and a half centuries old, still stands at the edge of a public road, defending itself against tourists who keep stripping its bark for souvenirs.
meta_description: Sintra's seven most remarkable trees: an 800-year sweet chestnut, a walking cedar at Pena and a 350-year cork oak fighting off souvenir hunters.
question_meta: Sintra's oldest tree is a sweet chestnut of about 800 years, its crown cut back in 2025 and still in leaf. Its story and six more remarkable trees.
question_answer: Sintra's oldest tree is the Sweet Chestnut of Caminho dos Frades, protected as a tree of public interest since 1945; Portugal's forestry register puts it at about 800 years, and the local tree group GAAS at more than 600. It stands on private ground at Quinta do Castanheiro, seen over the wall from the public lane.
question_context: It came through eight centuries and then, in February 2025, a cut that took its crown back to the trunk. GAAS took the case to the public prosecutor, saying the forestry service never approved the work; a local guide's photograph from November 2026 shows the twisted trunk above the estate wall with green growth above it. The register last measured it in 1989, at 9.6 metres round at chest height. Sintra's next oldest is the Fern Cork Oak near Quinta do Relógio, around 350 years by the same register, at the roadside on the way to Seteais, where tour guides have walked groups up to strip its bark. The rest are younger: a plane tree in Parque da Liberdade classified in 1951, and the imports of the Romantic gardens, a pohutukawa and a Norfolk Island pine at Monserrate and a walking cedar at Pena that has spent a century and a half rooting its own branches into the lawn. A Moreton Bay fig in Parque da Liberdade has no recorded age. The chestnut, the cork oak, the plane and the fig are free to see; Monserrate and Pena charge park admission.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Sintra?
faq.a: The Sweet Chestnut of Caminho dos Frades, protected since 1945 and put at about 800 years by Portugal's ICNF register, more than 600 by the tree group GAAS. Its crown was cut back in February 2025; it stands on private ground and is seen from the public lane outside. The Fern Cork Oak near Quinta do Relógio, about 350, comes next.

faq.q: Why is Sintra's cork oak losing its bark?
faq.a: Tour guides have taken to walking groups up to the Fern Cork Oak and encouraging them to strip off pieces of bark as souvenirs. The environmental association GAAS has publicly said the fencing the state put up around it does nothing to stop the damage.

faq.q: Why does the walking tree in Parque da Pena move?
faq.a: Its low branches arc down under their own weight, touch the ground, take root, and thicken into new trunks separate from the original. Repeated for about 150 years, the tree has visibly migrated several metres across its own patch of the park.

faq.q: Are Sintra's remarkable trees free to see?
faq.a: Four are: the cork oak near Quinta do Relógio and the plane tree and Moreton Bay fig in Parque da Liberdade, all outdoors in public spaces, and the sweet chestnut on Caminho dos Frades, seen from the lane. The pohutukawa and Norfolk Island pine at Monserrate and the walking cedar at Pena both require a paid park ticket.

trees.name: The Walking Tree of Pena

location.address: Parque da Pena, near the Fonte dos Passarinhos, 2710-609 Sintra

trees.story: This tree has spent a century and a half slowly relocating itself. Planted not long after King Ferdinand II began building his Romantic fantasy palace on the ruins of a monastery above Sintra, this western red cedar grows a peculiar habit into every low branch: instead of staying airborne, they arc down under their own weight, touch the ground, take root, and thicken into new trunks entirely separate from the original. Repeat that for a century and a half and the result is a small forest walking, metre by metre, toward the nearby lake, each generation of trunks a few steps closer than the last. Forestry students have used it as a teaching example since at least 1916, and it was still notable enough in 2019 to be shortlisted for Portugal's national Árvore do Ano contest. Its perimeter now measures nearly 17 metres, though that number describes a cluster of connected trunks rather than one column the way most tree measurements do. Parque da Pena's own guides call it simply the tree that walks, and once you have seen one root touch down mid-arc, the name stops sounding like a metaphor. It stands a short walk from the Fonte dos Passarinhos, inside the park surrounding Pena Palace, one of the most visited sites in Portugal.
trees.access: Paid entry: a Pena Park ticket (EUR 12 adult, EUR 10 ages 6 to 17 and over 65, under 6 free, per Parques de Sintra). The park is open 09:00 to 19:00, last entry 18:00, and the tree stands by the Fonte dos Passarinhos inside it.
trees.transport: Bus 434 (Pena Circuit) from Sintra train station, about 15 min
trees.notes: Age and history corroborated independently by Parques de Sintra's own blog and Ambiente Magazine's 2019 Arvore do Ano coverage (also carried by Sintra Noticias); no source gives an exact planting date, so the range is estimated from the park's mid-19th century construction under Ferdinand II. Photo viewed directly (fetched and read as an image, not just metadata): shows a multi-trunked conifer with one low branch arcing down and rooting into a new trunk beside an interpretive sign, matching this tree's own defining feature exactly. Coordinates tightened 2026-07-30, moved about 50m from the old Fonte dos Passarinhos landmark estimate: an OpenStreetMap node individually tagged 'Tuia-gigante' / 'Western Red Cedar' with a natural_monument denotation (Portugal's own tree-of-the-year competition once profiled it, though that specific page no longer resolves) sits at 38.786, -9.393361, matching this tree's species exactly. Portugal's ICNF national register of classified public-interest trees was checked directly for Sintra concelho (16 entries) and does not include this specimen, since it stands inside the paid Pena estate rather than on public land, so ICNF is not a competing source here.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its branches, arcing down to touch the ground and rooting into new trunks of their own. It stands near the Fonte dos Passarinhos, in Parque da Pena.

trees.name: The Fern Cork Oak of Quinta do Relógio
trees.age_estimate: more than 300 years, Portugal's own register puts it at 350

location.address: Roadside near Quinta do Relógio, Rua Barbosa du Bocage, 2710 Sintra

trees.story: Ferns grow straight out of this oak's bark, which is where its name comes from: Sobreira dos Fetos, the Fern Cork Oak. Portugal's forestry service classified it as a tree of public interest in 1996, by which point it had already stood beside the road to Seteais for roughly three centuries, older than the palace hotel that road now leads to. The English Romantic poet Robert Southey is said to have written that a painter should cross the Channel for no other reason than to see it, a claim that has outlived any record of when he supposedly made it. What has not faded is a more recent, less flattering kind of attention: tour guides have taken to walking groups up to the trunk to peel off pieces of bark as souvenirs, and the environmental association GAAS has publicly said the fencing the state put up around it does nothing to stop them. The tree stands on private land, but right at the roadside, visible and reachable from the public street rather than behind any gate, which is exactly why the damage keeps happening. It has stood here for three and a half centuries, and the thing most likely to cut that short is not age. It's whoever walks up next with a knife.
trees.access: Free, viewable from the public road; please don't touch or remove bark, the tree is under active pressure from souvenir stripping
trees.transport: 20 min walk from Sintra train station, on the road toward Seteais Palace

trees.name: The Plane Tree of Parque da Liberdade
trees.story: Sintra's park changed its name overnight and this tree didn't notice. Portuguese record keepers classified it as a tree of public interest in 1951, decades before 25 April 1974, when thousands of Sintra's own residents flooded this same municipal garden to celebrate the end of the dictatorship and the park was renamed Parque da Liberdade, Liberty Park, that same year. The tree itself, a London plane with a trunk measuring nearly ten metres around at its base, had already been growing for a century by then, planted sometime in the early to mid-1800s depending on which record you trust. The official government register puts it at roughly 200 years old, while a local history blog's own measurements suggest closer to 150. Either figure makes it one of the thickest plane trees documented anywhere in Portugal, rivalled mainly by a single private specimen near Figueira da Foz. Locals just call it the Platano Gigante, the giant plane, and treat the ground beneath it as one more park bench, shaded regardless of the hour by a canopy that has had a century and a half, at minimum, to fill in.

trees.name: The Araucaria of Monserrate

location.address: Parque de Monserrate, near the lake, 2710-405 Sintra

trees.story: The tallest tree in one of Portugal's most exotic gardens came from an island most of its visitors couldn't place on a map. Francis Cook, the English textile magnate who bought the crumbling Monserrate estate in 1856, spent the following decades turning its grounds into a private arboretum stitched together from wherever his money could reach: Mexico, the Himalayas, Australia, and this Araucaria heterophylla, native only to a single island in the Tasman Sea, Norfolk Island, some 1,600 kilometres from the Australian mainland it is usually filed under. Planted in Monserrate's mid-19th century expansion, it now stands over 50 metres tall with a crown spreading 22 metres across, by most measurements the tallest tree in the entire garden and a strong candidate for the tallest on mainland Portugal. It grows at the low point of the grounds, beside the ornamental lake, so that visitors coming down through Cook's Himalayan and Mexican plantings see it rising above everything else before they reach the water. Cook never lived to see the tree reach anything like its current size. What he built instead was a garden designed to keep growing into something stranger than he planted, and this conifer, alone among everything else at Monserrate, decided to do that by going straight up.
trees.access: Paid entry: a Monserrate ticket (EUR 12 adult, EUR 10 ages 6 to 17 and over 65, family EUR 33, per Parques de Sintra). The park is open 09:00 to 19:00, last entry 18:00; the ticket office closes 12:00 to 13:00 and a ticket machine is available.

trees.notes: Height and 'tallest in the garden' claim corroborated independently by Parques de Sintra's own site and the Almanaque Acoriano forestry article, which together also supply the mid-19th century, Francis Cook-era planting context; monumentaltrees.com's own estimate (germination around 1790) was checked for cross-verification only per hard rule 1 and not used, since it conflicts with both citable sources and cannot be independently confirmed. Photo viewed directly: a single tall conifer towering above the surrounding tree line next to a lake, matching 'at its base, next to the lake' exactly. Coordinates tightened 2026-07-30, moved about 120m from the palace's own generic coordinate: an OpenStreetMap node individually tagged 'Araucaria de Norfolk' with height=50m sits at 38.79332, -9.421356, matching this entry's own '50 metres tall' claim exactly and consistent with the lakeside location. Not on Portugal's ICNF public-interest register (checked directly for Sintra concelho, 16 entries, none matching), expected since the tree stands inside the paid Monserrate estate rather than on public land.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the tallest tree in the garden, over 50 metres, rising above everything around the lake. It stands beside the ornamental lake in Parque de Monserrate.

trees.name: The Pohutukawa of Monserrate
trees.age_estimate: genuinely uncertain, estimated between 175 and 275 years

best_time.label: late May and June, when it blooms scarlet, six months off the New Zealand summer it evolved for

trees.story: New Zealand's Christmas tree blooms scarlet in Portugal in early summer instead, six months off its native schedule and a hemisphere away from the only place it grows wild. This Metrosideros excelsa, a pohutukawa, is one of a pair planted in the grounds Francis Cook built around Monserrate Palace in the second half of the 19th century, though no record pins the planting to a specific year; estimates for this specimen, known locally only as New Zealand Two, range across a full century, sometime between 1750 and 1850, wide enough that even Monserrate's own material describes it simply as older than Cook's own tenure rather than assigning it a date. What is measured rather than estimated is its girth, just over 9 metres around a trunk that has grown the tangled aerial roots the species uses in the wild to grip volcanic coastal cliffs, here gripping nothing but Portuguese hillside soil a mountain away from any coastline. In New Zealand the tree is a national symbol, its flowering timed so precisely to the southern hemisphere summer that it marks the calendar the way certain trees elsewhere mark autumn. Cook's Monserrate collects that kind of geographic joke throughout its grounds, a garden built to prove a 19th century Englishman could grow almost anything on a hillside above Lisbon, if he imported the whole world to do it.
trees.access: Paid entry: a Monserrate ticket (EUR 12 adult, EUR 10 ages 6 to 17 and over 65, family EUR 33, per Parques de Sintra). The park is open 09:00 to 19:00, last entry 18:00; the ticket office closes 12:00 to 13:00 and a ticket machine is available.
trees.transport: Bus 435 (Monserrate Circuit) from Sintra train station, about 15 min
trees.notes: Location is approximate: no source gives surveyed coordinates for this individual specimen among Monserrate's two pohutukawa, so this uses the palace's own coordinate. Only one independent source found (Talking Plants blog, girth 9m/height 19.9m), which itself cites monumentaltrees.com; monumentaltrees was checked for cross-verification only per hard rule 1, never copied or cited directly. A second, larger specimen at Monserrate ('New Zealand One', girth 12.75m per monumentaltrees) was deliberately not used as a second entry: no independent source distinguishes it from this one, and running with monumentaltrees as the sole source for a second tree would fail the two-source bar this project holds to. Flagged for single-source age and the wide 1750-1850 planting estimate, honestly stated rather than narrowed. No open-licensed photo found on Wikimedia Commons, iNaturalist (only CC-BY-NC and all-rights-reserved observations of this species near Sintra) or Flickr; genuinely missing.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, just over nine metres round and tangled with aerial roots, and by the scarlet flowers in early summer. It is one of a pair, the one recorded as New Zealand Two.

trees.name: The Moreton Bay Fig of Parque da Liberdade
trees.story:
Roots drop from high in this Moreton Bay fig's crown and run down its trunk, fused and braided over one another until the stem looks more like a bundle of roots than a single trunk, then spread over the ground at its foot in thick, mossy buttresses. The species comes from the rainforests of eastern Australia. This one grows in Parque da Liberdade, Sintra's municipal park, about thirty metres from the town's giant plane tree.

A nature guide who lives in Sintra and leads seasonal walks among the town's trees sent it to us in November 2026, with the photograph on this page and the spot where it stands. That is the whole of its written record so far: we found no register entry, no measurement and no planting date, so this page makes no claim about its age. What the photograph does show is the braided base, a tangle of roots holding up the trunk, and a crown of large, leathery leaves above the path. If you know when it was planted, or how big it is around, tell us.

trees.name: The Sweet Chestnut of Caminho dos Frades
trees.age_estimate: about 800 years by Portugal's register, more than 600 by the local tree group GAAS

location.address: Caminho dos Frades, outside the wall of Quinta do Castanheiro, 2710 Sintra

trees.story:
Portugal's forestry register puts this sweet chestnut at about 800 years old, and the local tree group GAAS calls it the oldest tree in the municipality. It has been protected as a tree of public interest since 1945. When the register last measured it, in 1989, the trunk was 9.6 metres round at chest height and 10.2 metres at the base.

In February 2025 its crown was cut back to the trunk. GAAS, which puts its age at more than six hundred years, took the case to the public prosecutor, saying the forestry service had not approved the work and warning that the few young shoots left might not be enough to keep it alive. The estate's stated reason was that the trunk was cracking a wall and its heavy limbs were a risk.

A nature guide who lives in Sintra photographed it for us in November 2026. The twisted, hollowed trunk rises above the estate wall, and green leafy growth stands above it. The tree is on private ground at Quinta do Castanheiro. You see it from Caminho dos Frades, the lane outside, which is where the pin stands.
